strategy_title: Incremental Autotune Config Expansion Yields Negligible Gain
strategy_description: Adding 4 more autotune configs (BLOCK_N=128/256/512/1024 with varied num_stages=2/3 and num_warps=4/8) to an already-expanded Triton autotune list produced essentially no measurable improvement: duration changed from 618.75µs to 616.58µs (~0.35% improvement within noise), and all key metrics (compute throughput, occupancy, register count, scheduler eligibility) remained statistically identical. The L2 hit rate improved marginally (81.26% → 89.03%), but this did not translate to meaningful latency reduction. When the kernel is already register- and SMEM-limited to 2 blocks/SM (Theoretical Occupancy 12.5%), incremental config additions that do not change the binding occupancy constraints cannot improve performance — the autotuner has already converged to the optimal config within the structural constraints.
slow_pseudocode:
# 8 autotune configs: BLOCK_N in {512,1024,2048,256,128,256,512,1024}, num_stages=2/3, num_warps=4/8/16
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 512},  num_stages=2, num_warps=8),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 1024}, num_stages=2, num_warps=8),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 2048}, num_stages=2, num_warps=16),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 256},  num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 128},  num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 256},  num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 512},  num_stages=3, num_warps=8),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 1024}, num_stages=3, num_warps=8),
], key=['N'])
fast_pseudocode:
# 12 autotune configs: added 4 more BLOCK_N/num_stages/num_warps combos
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 512},  num_stages=2, num_warps=8),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 1024}, num_stages=2, num_warps=8),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 2048}, num_stages=2, num_warps=16),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 256},  num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 128},  num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 256},  num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 512},  num_stages=3, num_warps=8),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 1024}, num_stages=3, num_warps=8),
    # NEW configs — negligible improvement
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 128},  num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 256},  num_stages=3, num_warps=8),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 512},  num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 1024}, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
], key=['N'])
applicable_when: Autotune config space has not yet been explored at all; kernel has not been autotuned with any configs; first-time autotune addition where the config space is genuinely unexplored.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel is already register- and SMEM-limited to 2 blocks/SM (Block Limit Registers=2, Block Limit Shared Mem=2, Theoretical Occupancy=12.5%); the existing autotune config space already covers the relevant BLOCK_N/num_stages/num_warps ranges; incremental config additions that do not change the binding occupancy limiter will not improve performance and only increase autotuning search time.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: when Block Limit Registers and Block Limit Shared Mem are both at 2 blocks/SM, the kernel is doubly constrained. Adding configs with the same BLOCK sizes and num_stages will not break either constraint. To escape this ceiling, configs must either reduce BLOCK_M/BLOCK_N (lower register pressure) or reduce num_stages (lower SMEM usage) — but both risk reducing arithmetic intensity per CTA and lowering Compute (SM) Throughput.

strategy_title: Comment Removal in Autotune Configs Yields No Meaningful Gain
strategy_description: The actual code diff between the slow and fast kernels in this iteration consists entirely of removing inline comments from the @triton.autotune config list — no functional code was changed. All launch parameters (block_size=128, grid_size=512, registers_per_thread=198, dynamic_smem=98.3 KB, waves_per_sm=1.94) are identical before and after, and all profiling metrics changed by less than 1% (Duration: 618.75 µs → 618.18 µs, Compute SM Throughput: 59.87% → 60.47%). The reported 12.9x speedup reflects the cumulative gain from prior iterations (TF32 enablement, autotune expansion) that were already baked into the 'before' kernel of this iteration, not from the comment removal itself. Removing comments from autotune config lists has zero performance impact; the speedup number here is an artifact of the measurement baseline.
slow_pseudocode:
# Autotune configs with inline comments
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    triton.Config({...}, num_stages=4, num_warps=8),
    # NEW: larger BLOCK_K, more stages, higher num_warps for H200 Tensor Core saturation
    triton.Config({...}, num_stages=4, num_warps=8),
    # num_stages=2: halve SMEM per block (~98KB->~49KB)
    triton.Config({...}, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
    # GROUP_M=4/16: align tile grouping with 132-SM wave boundary
    triton.Config({...}, num_stages=3, num_warps=8),
    # NEW: explore BLOCK_N=128 and 512 with varied num_warps
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 128}, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
], key=['M','N','K'])
fast_pseudocode:
# Identical autotune configs, comments removed — no functional change
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    triton.Config({...}, num_stages=4, num_warps=8),
    triton.Config({...}, num_stages=4, num_warps=8),
    triton.Config({...}, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),

    triton.Config({'BLOCK_N': 128}, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),

applicable_when: Never — comment removal has no performance impact under any conditions.
do_not_apply_when: Always: removing comments from autotune config lists is a no-op. Do not attribute speedup to this change. The 12.9x speedup in this iteration is inherited from prior TF32 + autotune expansion changes, not from comment removal.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: @triton.autotune config lists are Python data structures; inline comments are stripped at parse time and have zero effect on compiled kernel behavior, register allocation, shared memory usage, or autotuner search space.

strategy_title: Online Logsumexp Single-Pass Yields No Measurable Gain
strategy_description: Replacing a two-pass logsumexp (separate max and sum-exp loops) with a single-pass online algorithm was expected to halve memory traffic for the reduction kernel, but the profiling data shows essentially no change across all metrics: Duration increased slightly (618 µs → 626 µs), Executed Instructions are identical (115,308,544), DRAM Throughput is unchanged (12.26% → 11.92%), and L2 Hit Rate is nearly identical (81.26% → 82.06%). The diff shows an empty code change, indicating the optimization was either not applied or the reduction kernel's memory traffic is negligible relative to the dominant matmul kernel, making the two-pass vs. one-pass distinction irrelevant to end-to-end latency. This strategy is ineffective when the profiled kernel is the matmul (not the reduction), and the reduction kernel's contribution to total runtime is too small to measure.
slow_pseudocode:
# Two-pass logsumexp: reads mm_out buffer twice
row_max = -inf
for off in range(0, N, BLOCK_N):  # Pass 1: compute max
    val = load(mm_ptr + row*N + cols)
    row_max = max(row_max, max(val))
row_sum = 0
for off in range(0, N, BLOCK_N):  # Pass 2: compute sum(exp(x - max))
    val = load(mm_ptr + row*N + cols)  # second read
    row_sum += sum(exp(val - row_max))
lse = log(row_sum) + row_max
fast_pseudocode:
# Single-pass online logsumexp: reads mm_out buffer once
row_max = -inf
row_sum = 0
for off in range(0, N, BLOCK_N):  # Single pass
    val = load(mm_ptr + row*N + cols)  # one read
    local_max = max(val)
    new_max = max(row_max, local_max)
    row_sum = row_sum * exp(row_max - new_max) + sum(exp(val - new_max))
    row_max = new_max
lse = log(row_sum) + row_max
applicable_when: The reduction kernel (logsumexp/softmax) is the dominant contributor to end-to-end latency; the buffer being read twice is large enough to cause measurable DRAM traffic (e.g., exceeds L2 cache capacity); profiling shows the reduction kernel specifically has high DRAM throughput and two distinct load phases for the same buffer
do_not_apply_when: The profiled kernel is the matmul (not the reduction); the reduction kernel's runtime is negligible compared to the matmul kernel; the buffer being read twice fits entirely in L2 cache (L2 Hit Rate >80% means the second pass is served from cache, not DRAM); the code diff is empty (change was not actually applied); all key metrics (Duration, Executed Instructions, DRAM Throughput) are identical before and after
framework_notes: The empty diff suggests the change was not actually applied to the kernel. When the reduction kernel's buffer fits in L2 (81% hit rate), the second pass incurs L2 hits rather than DRAM reads, making the two-pass vs. one-pass distinction irrelevant to memory bandwidth. The online logsumexp algorithm is mathematically sound but only provides speedup when the second pass causes real DRAM traffic.

strategy_title: Replace Two-Pass LogSumExp with Online Single-Pass Algorithm
strategy_description: A two-pass logsumexp reduction (pass 1: compute row max; pass 2: re-read all data to compute sum(exp(x - max))) reads the input buffer twice, doubling L2/DRAM traffic. Replacing it with the online (Milakov-Norouzi) algorithm — maintaining running (max, sum_exp) state and merging each tile via the numerically stable rescaling formula — eliminates the second full pass and halves memory traffic from the reduction kernel. This is most impactful when the input buffer is large enough to saturate L2 (e.g., 32 MB on a 50 MB L2 cache), causing L2 Cache Throughput to approach or exceed 80% and SOLBottleneck to identify memory as the binding limiter. The merge formula per tile is: new_max = max(old_max, tile_max); new_sum = old_sum * exp(old_max - new_max) + tile_sum * exp(tile_max - new_max), where tile_sum = sum(exp(val - tile_max)) to prevent overflow.
slow_pseudocode:
# Two-pass logsumexp: reads input buffer TWICE
# Pass 1: compute row max
row_max = float('-inf')
for off in range(0, N, BLOCK_N):
    val = load_and_transform(input[row, off:off+BLOCK_N])  # 1st read
    row_max = max(row_max, tile_max(val))
row_max_safe = 0.0 if abs(row_max)==inf else row_max
# Pass 2: compute sum_exp (re-reads entire input)
row_sum = 0.0
for off in range(0, N, BLOCK_N):
    val = load_and_transform(input[row, off:off+BLOCK_N])  # 2nd read
    row_sum += sum(exp(val - row_max_safe))
lse = log(row_sum) + row_max_safe
fast_pseudocode:
# Single-pass online logsumexp: reads input buffer ONCE
running_max = float('-inf')
running_sum = 0.0
for off in range(0, N, BLOCK_N):
    val = load_and_transform(input[row, off:off+BLOCK_N], other=float('-inf'))  # 1 read only
    tile_max = max(val[mask], -inf)
    tile_sum = sum(exp(val - tile_max) where mask else 0.0)
    new_max = max(running_max, tile_max)
    running_sum = (running_sum * exp(running_max - new_max)
                 + tile_sum   * exp(tile_max    - new_max))
    running_max = new_max
running_max_safe = 0.0 if abs(running_max)==inf else running_max
lse = log(running_sum) + running_max_safe
applicable_when: A reduction kernel performs two sequential passes over the same large input buffer (e.g., logsumexp, softmax normalization); L2 Cache Throughput > 75% and SOLBottleneck identifies memory as the binding limiter; L2 Hit Rate > 80% (data is L2-resident but L2 is saturated); the input buffer size is a significant fraction of the L2 cache size; MemoryL2Compression rule fires with 0% compression success confirming L2 is the bottleneck
do_not_apply_when: The reduction is already single-pass; the input buffer is small enough that both passes fit comfortably in L2 without saturation (L2 Cache Throughput < 50%); the kernel is compute-bound rather than memory-bound (Compute SM Throughput > 80%); numerical precision requirements prohibit the online rescaling (though the algorithm is mathematically exact in floating point up to rounding)
framework_notes: Triton-specific: use other=float('-inf') (not 0.0) when loading masked lanes for mm_val so that exp(-inf - tile_max) = 0 contributes nothing to tile_sum. Use tl.exp() for tile-level exp and tl.max()/tl.sum() for reductions. The online algorithm adds ~2 extra tl.exp() calls per tile for rescaling (running_sum * exp(old_max - new_max) and tile_sum * exp(tile_max - new_max)) but these are negligible vs. the 50% memory traffic reduction. In CUDA, the equivalent is the Milakov-Norouzi online softmax algorithm used in FlashAttention.

strategy_title: tl.make_block_ptr Swizzle on Already-TF32 Kernel Yields Marginal Gain
strategy_description: Replacing manual pointer arithmetic (offs_k + stride-based A_ptrs/B_ptrs) with tl.make_block_ptr(..., order=(1,0)/(0,1)) in a Triton matmul kernel that already uses allow_tf32=True produced only a ~0.07% duration improvement (616.58 µs → 616.16 µs), well within measurement noise. While NCU's SharedMemoryConflicts rule fired after the change (5x average bank conflict, 10.68% excess wavefronts), the instruction count dropped from 115M to 100M, suggesting the compiler generated fewer instructions via block pointer paths — yet Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction worsened (7.19 → 8.20) and Eligible Warps Per Scheduler decreased (0.34 → 0.29), indicating the make_block_ptr path introduced additional fixed-latency stalls that offset the bank-conflict reduction. When the kernel is already register- and SMEM-limited to 2 blocks/SM with Tensor Cores active, the shared memory pipeline is not the binding bottleneck and swizzle provides negligible benefit.
slow_pseudocode:
# Manual pointer arithmetic — no automatic smem swizzle
offs_k = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K)
A_ptrs = A_ptr + offs_m[:, None] * stride_am + offs_k[None, :] * stride_ak
B_ptrs = B_ptr + offs_k[:, None] * stride_bk + offs_n[None, :] * stride_bn
for k in range(0, tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
    k_remaining = K - k * BLOCK_K
    a = tl.load(A_ptrs, mask=(offs_m[:,None]<M)&(offs_k[None,:]<k_remaining), other=0.0)
    b = tl.load(B_ptrs, mask=(offs_k[:,None]<k_remaining)&(offs_n[None,:]<N), other=0.0)
    acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc, allow_tf32=True)
    A_ptrs += BLOCK_K * stride_ak
    B_ptrs += BLOCK_K * stride_bk
fast_pseudocode:
# tl.make_block_ptr with order hints — compiler inserts smem swizzle
A_block_ptr = tl.make_block_ptr(
    base=A_ptr, shape=(M, K), strides=(stride_am, stride_ak),
    offsets=(pid_m * BLOCK_M, 0), block_shape=(BLOCK_M, BLOCK_K),
    order=(1, 0),
)
B_block_ptr = tl.make_block_ptr(
    base=B_ptr, shape=(K, N), strides=(stride_bk, stride_bn),
    offsets=(0, pid_n * BLOCK_N), block_shape=(BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N),
    order=(0, 1),
)
for k in range(0, tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
    a = tl.load(A_block_ptr, boundary_check=(0, 1), padding_option='zero')
    b = tl.load(B_block_ptr, boundary_check=(0, 1), padding_option='zero')
    acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc, allow_tf32=True)
    A_block_ptr = tl.advance(A_block_ptr, (0, BLOCK_K))
    B_block_ptr = tl.advance(B_block_ptr, (BLOCK_K, 0))
applicable_when: NCU reports SharedMemoryConflicts with >5x average bank conflict way AND the kernel is NOT already Tensor-Core-bound with allow_tf32=True; the shared pipeline is the highest-utilized pipeline (>60%) AND the kernel has meaningful headroom in Eligible Warps Per Scheduler (>0.4); the kernel is not already doubly constrained by both register and SMEM limits at 2 blocks/SM
do_not_apply_when: Kernel already uses allow_tf32=True and is Tensor-Core-bound (Compute SM Throughput ~60%, Block Limit Registers=2, Block Limit Shared Mem=2, Theoretical Occupancy=12.5%); Eligible Warps Per Scheduler is already low (<0.35) — the make_block_ptr path can worsen Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction by introducing additional fixed-latency stalls; the expected speedup from bank-conflict reduction is <5% (marginal relative to noise floor); the kernel has already been profiled and the shared pipeline is not the binding bottleneck
framework_notes: Triton-specific: tl.make_block_ptr with order=(1,0) for row-major A and order=(0,1) for col-major B triggers automatic shared memory swizzle insertion. On Hopper (sm_90a), this also enables TMA async copy paths when num_stages>=2. However, when the kernel is already register+SMEM limited to 2 blocks/SM with Tensor Cores active, the TMA path does not provide additional latency hiding beyond what the existing software pipeline achieves. The boundary_check=(0,1) with padding_option='zero' replaces manual mask arithmetic but adds boundary-check overhead. The instruction count reduction (115M→100M) from make_block_ptr does not translate to latency improvement when Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction increases proportionally.

strategy_title: Cap SMEM < 76KB to Unlock 3+ Blocks Per SM on H200
strategy_description: When a Triton matmul kernel is doubly constrained by Block Limit Registers=2 AND Block Limit Shared Mem=2 (Theoretical Occupancy=12.5%), replacing all autotune configs with entries satisfying num_stages×(BLOCK_M×BLOCK_K + BLOCK_K×BLOCK_N)×4 < 76,800 bytes (the H200 threshold for 3 blocks/SM with 228 KB SMEM/SM) breaks the SMEM ceiling: Block Limit Shared Mem rose from 2 to 4, Theoretical Occupancy doubled from 12.5% to 25%, Active Warps Per Scheduler nearly doubled (1.98→3.76), and Eligible Warps Per Scheduler improved from 0.34 to 0.85. However, the smaller tiles reduced arithmetic intensity per CTA, shifting the kernel from compute-bound (Compute SM Throughput 60%→46%) to more memory-bound (Memory Throughput 56%→82%), and the winning config (SMEM=49 KB, registers=64) increased kernel duration from 617 µs to 832 µs despite better occupancy — the net effect was a regression relative to the prior best (12.94x), yielding only 9.60x speedup. The occupancy gain was real but insufficient to compensate for the arithmetic intensity loss from smaller tiles.
fast_pseudocode:
# After: small tiles, low SMEM (49-66 KB/block), 4 blocks/SM, 25% occupancy
# Block Limit Shared Mem=4, Block Limit Registers=8
# BUT: smaller tiles reduce arithmetic intensity -> kernel becomes more memory-bound
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    # All configs satisfy: num_stages*(BLOCK_M*BLOCK_K + BLOCK_K*BLOCK_N)*4 < 76800
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64,  'BLOCK_N': 64,  'BLOCK_K': 32, 'GROUP_M': 8}, num_stages=3, num_warps=4),  # 49152 bytes
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 128, 'BLOCK_K': 32, 'GROUP_M': 8}, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),  # 65536 bytes
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64,  'BLOCK_N': 64,  'BLOCK_K': 64, 'GROUP_M': 8}, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),  # 65536 bytes
    # ... all configs with SMEM < 76800 bytes
], key=['M', 'N', 'K'])
applicable_when: Triton matmul where Block Limit Shared Mem is the sole binding occupancy limiter (Block Limit Registers > Block Limit Shared Mem); problem size is large enough that smaller tiles still maintain arithmetic intensity above the memory ridge point; the target occupancy tier (e.g., 3 blocks/SM) can be reached without reducing tile sizes so much that the kernel becomes memory-bandwidth-bound
do_not_apply_when: Block Limit Registers is co-equal or lower than Block Limit Shared Mem (both=2 as in this case) — reducing SMEM alone won't help if registers remain the binding limiter; the problem size or matrix dimensions are such that smaller tiles (e.g., BLOCK_M=64, BLOCK_N=64) reduce arithmetic intensity below the ridge point, making the kernel memory-bound and increasing duration despite better occupancy; the prior best config already achieves high Compute SM Throughput (>55%) with 2 blocks/SM — the occupancy gain from 3 blocks/SM may not compensate for the arithmetic intensity loss
framework_notes: Triton-specific: SMEM per block = num_stages × (BLOCK_M × BLOCK_K + BLOCK_K × BLOCK_N) × sizeof(dtype). On H200 (228 KB/SM): threshold for 2 blocks/SM = 114 KB; for 3 blocks/SM = 76 KB; for 4 blocks/SM = 57 KB. In this case, the winning config used 49 KB (4 blocks/SM possible), but the smaller tiles (BLOCK_M=64, BLOCK_N=64 or similar) reduced Compute SM Throughput from 60% to 46% and increased duration. The key lesson: when both Block Limit Registers AND Block Limit Shared Mem are at 2, the kernel is doubly constrained and reducing SMEM alone (without also reducing register pressure proportionally) may not yield net improvement if the tile size reduction causes an arithmetic intensity cliff.

strategy_title: Smaller Autotune Tile Configs Halve Register Count, Shift Bottleneck
strategy_description: Replacing large-tile autotune configs (BLOCK_M=128/256, BLOCK_N=128/256, BLOCK_K=64/128 with num_warps=8/16) with smaller-tile configs (BLOCK_M=64/128, BLOCK_N=64/128, BLOCK_K=32/64 with num_warps=4/8) caused the autotuner to select a config that halved registers per thread from 198 to 95, relaxing Block Limit Registers from 2 to 5 blocks/SM. This shifted the binding occupancy limiter from registers to shared memory (Block Limit Shared Mem=2), increased grid size from 512 to 2048 (waves_per_SM: 1.94→7.76), and raised memory throughput from 56% to 83%. However, the kernel duration increased (617µs→854µs) because the smaller tiles reduced arithmetic intensity per CTA, lowering Compute SM Throughput from 60% to 45% and shifting the kernel from compute-bound to memory-bound — a net regression in this case. The speedup figure (9.35x) reflects the cumulative baseline from prior iterations, not this specific change.
slow_pseudocode:
# Large-tile autotune configs: high register pressure, low grid coverage
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 128, 'BLOCK_K': 64,  'GROUP_M': 8}, num_stages=4, num_warps=8),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 256, 'BLOCK_K': 64,  'GROUP_M': 8}, num_stages=4, num_warps=8),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 256, 'BLOCK_N': 128, 'BLOCK_K': 64,  'GROUP_M': 8}, num_stages=4, num_warps=8),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 256, 'BLOCK_N': 128, 'BLOCK_K': 128, 'GROUP_M': 8}, num_stages=4, num_warps=16),
    # ... 198 registers/thread, grid=512, waves=1.94
], key=['M','N','K'])
fast_pseudocode:
# Smaller-tile autotune configs: lower register pressure, higher grid coverage
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64,  'BLOCK_N': 64,  'BLOCK_K': 64,  'GROUP_M': 8}, num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 64,  'BLOCK_K': 64,  'GROUP_M': 8}, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64,  'BLOCK_N': 128, 'BLOCK_K': 32,  'GROUP_M': 8}, num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 128, 'BLOCK_K': 32,  'GROUP_M': 8}, num_stages=2, num_warps=8),
    # ... 95 registers/thread, grid=2048, waves=7.76
], key=['M','N','K'])
applicable_when: Register pressure is the sole binding occupancy limiter (Block Limit Registers < Block Limit Shared Mem); reducing tile sizes would not push the kernel into a memory-bandwidth-bound regime; the problem size is large enough that more waves (higher grid coverage) compensates for lower per-CTA arithmetic intensity.
do_not_apply_when: The kernel is already at the optimal compute-to-memory balance (Compute SM Throughput ~60%); reducing tile sizes shifts the bottleneck from compute to memory (L2/DRAM throughput rises above 80%) and increases duration; shared memory is already the binding occupancy limiter (Block Limit Shared Mem ≤ Block Limit Registers); the existing config already achieves good wave coverage (waves_per_SM > 4).
framework_notes: Triton-specific: the autotuner selects the winning config at runtime; replacing large-tile configs with smaller-tile configs does not guarantee the autotuner picks a smaller tile — it picks whichever is fastest. In this case the winning config after the change used BLOCK_M=128/BLOCK_N=64/BLOCK_K=64 (95 registers/thread vs. 198 before). On H200, Block Limit Registers dropping from 2 to 5 is a positive signal for occupancy, but if shared memory remains the binding limiter at 2 blocks/SM, the net occupancy gain is zero and the arithmetic intensity loss dominates.
